claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data, consistent with previous research.

claims.claim: All three D. simulans clade species still retain IGS repeats despite the loss of rRNA coding sequences.
claims.source: Our assemblies indicate that, despite this loss of the rRNA coding sequences, all three species still retain IGS repeats.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: Y-linked IGS repeats are not detected at the cytological level in D. sechellia, suggesting their abundance is below the level of detection by FISH.
claims.source: However, we and others do not detect Y-linked IGS repeats at the cytological level in D. sechellia (Figure 1—figure supplements 3–4; Roy et al., 2005; Lohe and Roberts, 2000; Lohe and Roberts, 1990), suggesting that their abundance is below the level of detection by FISH in this species.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on FISH data, with an inference about abundance.

claims.claim: Previous studies reported many duplications of canonical Y-linked genes in D. simulans.
claims.source: Previous studies reported many duplications of canonical Y-linked genes in D. simulans (Helleu et al., 2019; Chakraborty et al., 2021; Kopp et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: All three D. simulans clade species have at least one intact copy of the 11 canonical Y-linked genes.
claims.source: We find that all three species have at least one intact copy of the 11 canonical Y-linked genes, but there is also extensive copy number variation in Y-linked exons across these species (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2; Supplementary file 1; Chakraborty, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: There is extensive copy number variation in Y-linked exons across the three D. simulans clade species.
claims.source: We find that all three species have at least one intact copy of the 11 canonical Y-linked genes, but there is also extensive copy number variation in Y-linked exons across these species (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2; Supplementary file 1; Chakraborty, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: Some duplicated Y-linked exons in D. sechellia, particularly in kl-3, WDY, and Ppr-Y, are not assembled.
claims.source: Using Illumina reads, we confirm the copy number variation in our assemblies and reveal some duplicated Y-linked exons, particularly in kl-3, WDY, and Ppr-Y, that are not assembled in D. sechellia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on Illumina sequencing data.

claims.claim: Some Y-linked gene duplicates may be functional because they are expressed and have complete open reading frames.
claims.source: Some duplicates may be functional because they are expressed and have complete open reading frames, (e.g. ARY, Ppr-Y1, and Ppr-Y2).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on expression and sequence data.

claims.claim: The D. simulans Y chromosome has four complete copies of ARY, all of which show similar expression levels from RNA-seq data.
claims.source: The D. simulans Y chromosome has four complete copies of ARY, all of which show similar expression levels from RNA-seq data (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 4), but two copies have inverted exons 1 and 2.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Two copies of ARY in D. simulans have inverted exons 1 and 2.
claims.source: The D. simulans Y chromosome has four complete copies of ARY, all of which show similar expression levels from RNA-seq data (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 4), but two copies have inverted exons 1 and 2.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: D. sechellia contains at least five duplicated copies of ARY, some of which also have the inverted exons 1 and 2.
claims.source: D. sechellia also contains at least five duplicated copies of ARY, some of which also have the inverted exons 1 and 2, but the absence of RNA-seq data from testes of this species prevents inferences regarding whether all copies of ARY are expressed.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: Most duplications of Y-linked genes include only a subset of exons, and in many cases, the duplicated exons are located on the periphery of the presumed functional gene copy.
claims.source: However, most duplications include only a subset of exons, and in many cases, the duplicated exons are located on the periphery of the presumed functional gene copy (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: Both D. simulans and D. mauritiana have multiple copies of exons 8–12 located at the 3' end of kl-2.
claims.source: For example, both D. simulans and D. mauritiana have multiple copies of exons 8–12 located at the 3' end of kl-2 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: In D. simulans, most of the extra exons of kl-2 have low to no expression.
claims.source: In D. simulans, most of these extra exons have low to no expression, while in D. mauritiana, there appears to be a substantial expression from many of the duplicated terminal exons, as well as an internal duplication of exon 5.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: In D. mauritiana, there appears to be substantial expression from many of the duplicated terminal exons of kl-2, as well as an internal duplication of exon 5.
claims.source: In D. simulans, most of these extra exons have low to no expression, while in D. mauritiana, there appears to be a substantial expression from many of the duplicated terminal exons, as well as an internal duplication of exon 5.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: It is unclear what effects duplicated exons have on the protein sequences of fertility-essential genes.
claims.source: Although the duplications of Y-linked genes can influence their expression, especially for genes with short introns (e.g. ARY, Ppr-Y1 and Ppr-Y2), it is unclear what effects these duplicated exons have on the protein sequences of these fertility-essential genes.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claims.claim: All exon-intron junctions are conserved within full-length copies of the canonical Y-linked genes.
claims.source: All exon-intron junctions are conserved within full-length copies of the canonical Y-linked genes, but intron lengths vary between these species (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: Intron lengths vary between the D. simulans clade species.
claims.source: All exon-intron junctions are conserved within full-length copies of the canonical Y-linked genes, but intron lengths vary between these species (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: The length of longer introns (> 100 bp in any species) is more dynamic than that of short introns.
claims.source: The length of longer introns ( > 100 bp in any species) is more dynamic than that of short introns (Figure 3; Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: The dramatic size differences in most introns cannot be attributed to a single deletion or duplication.
claims.source: The dramatic size differences in most introns cannot be attributed to a single deletion or duplication (see ORY example in Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on sequence alignment data.

claims.claim: Some Y-linked genes contain mega-base sized introns (i.e., mega-introns) whose transcription manifests as cytologically visible lampbrush-like loops (Y-loops) in primary spermatocytes.
claims.source: Some Y-linked genes contain mega-base sized introns (i.e., mega-introns) whose transcription manifests as cytologically visible lampbrush-like loops (Y-loops) in primary spermatocytes (Bonaccorsi et al., 1988; Bonaccorsi et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Y-loops are found across the Drosophila genus.
claims.source: While Y-loops are found across the Drosophila genus (Meyer, 1963; Piergentili, 2007), their potential functions are unknown (Fingerhut et al., 2019; Redhouse et al., 2011; Pisano et al., 1993; Piergentili et al., 2004; Piergentili and Mencarelli, 2008) and the genes/introns that produce Y-loops differs among species (Chang and Larracuente, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The potential functions of Y-loops are unknown.
claims.source: While Y-loops are found across the Drosophila genus (Meyer, 1963; Piergentili, 2007), their potential functions are unknown (Fingerhut et al., 2019; Redhouse et al., 2011; Pisano et al., 1993; Piergentili et al., 2004; Piergentili and Mencarelli, 2008) and the genes/introns that produce Y-loops differs among species (Chang and Larracuente, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The genes/introns that produce Y-loops differ among Drosophila species.
claims.source: While Y-loops are found across the Drosophila genus (Meyer, 1963; Piergentili, 2007), their potential functions are unknown (Fingerhut et al., 2019; Redhouse et al., 2011; Pisano et al., 1993; Piergentili et al., 2004; Piergentili and Mencarelli, 2008) and the genes/introns that produce Y-loops differs among species (Chang and Larracuente, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: D. melanogaster has three Y-loops transcribed from introns of ORY (ks-1 in previous literature), kl-3, and kl-5.
claims.source: D. melanogaster has three Y-loops transcribed from introns of ORY (ks-1 in previous literature), kl-3, and kl-5 (Bonaccorsi et al., 1988).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: D. simulans has three Y-loops based on cytological evidence.
claims.source: Based on cytological evidence, D. simulans has three Y-loops, whereas D. mauritiana and D. sechellia only have two (Piergentili, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: D. mauritiana and D. sechellia have two Y-loops based on cytological evidence.
claims.source: Based on cytological evidence, D. simulans has three Y-loops, whereas D. mauritiana and D. sechellia only have two (Piergentili, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Only the kl-3 mega-intron is conserved in all four species (D. melanogaster and the D. simulans clade) and has the same intron structure and sequences (i.e. (AATAT)n repeats).
claims.source: Of all potential loop-producing introns, we find that only the kl-3 mega-intron is conserved in all four species and has the same intron structure and sequences (i.e. (AATAT)n repeats).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: (AAGAC)n repeats are missing from the genomes of the D. simulans clade species.
claims.source: While both kl-5 and ORY produce Y-loops with (AAGAC)n repeats in D. melanogaster, (AAGAC)n is missing from the genomes of the D. simulans clade species. This observation is supported by our assemblies, the Illumina raw reads (Supplementary file 6), and published FISH results (Jagannathan et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly and sequencing data, supported by previous research.

claims.claim: In the D. simulans clade, the ORY introns do not carry any long tandem repeats.
claims.source: In the D. simulans clade, the ORY introns do not carry any long tandem repeats.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: kl-5 has introns with (AATAT)n repeats that may form a Y-loop in the D. simulans clade species.
claims.source: However, kl-5 has introns with (AATAT)n repeats that may form a Y-loop in the D. simulans clade species.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data, with speculation about Y-loop formation.

claims.claim: Mega-introns and Y-loops may be conserved features of spermatogenesis in Drosophila, but they turn over at both the sequence and gene levels over short periods of evolutionary time.
claims.source: These data suggest that, while mega-introns and Y-loops may be conserved features of spermatogenesis in Drosophila, they turn over at both the sequence and gene levels over short periods of evolutionary time (i.e. ~ 2 My between D. melanogaster and the D. simulans clade).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study.

claims.claim: The study identified high rates of gene duplication to the D. simulans clade Y chromosome from other chromosomes.
claims.source: Consistent with previous studies (Tobler et al., 2017; Chakraborty et al., 2021), we identify high rates of gene duplication to the D. simulans clade Y chromosome from other chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study, consistent with previous research.

claims.claim: The study found 49 independent duplications to the Y chromosome in the heterochromatin-enriched assemblies.
claims.source: We find 49 independent duplications to the Y chromosome in our heterochromatin-enriched assemblies (Figure 4; Supplementary file 7), including eight newly discovered duplications (Tobler et al., 2017; Chakraborty et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: Eight of the Y-linked duplications are newly discovered.
claims.source: We find 49 independent duplications to the Y chromosome in our heterochromatin-enriched assemblies (Figure 4; Supplementary file 7), including eight newly discovered duplications (Tobler et al., 2017; Chakraborty et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: Twenty-eight duplications to the Y chromosome are DNA-based, 13 are RNA-based, and the rest are unknown due to limited sequence information.
claims.source: Twenty-eight duplications are DNA-based, 13 are RNA-based, and the rest are unknown due to limited sequence information (Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: The rate of transposition to the Y chromosome is about three to four times higher in the D. simulans clade compared to D. melanogaster.
claims.source: The rate of transposition to the Y chromosome is about three to four times higher in the D. simulans clade compared to D. melanogaster (Chang and Larracuente, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on comparison with previous data.

claims.claim: 17 duplicated genes were independently deleted from D. simulans clade Y chromosomes.
claims.source: We also infer that 17 duplicated genes were independently deleted from D. simulans clade Y chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Some Y-linked duplications, including Fdy, Mst77Y and pirate, are known to be functional and/or under purifying selection.
claims.source: Some of these Y-linked duplications, including Fdy, Mst77Y and pirate, are known to be functional and/or under purifying selection (Tobler et al., 2017; Krsticevic et al., 2015; Russell and Kaiser, 1993; Chen et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: More than half of the duplicated genes are likely pseudogenes that either show no expression in testes (< 3 TPM) or lack open reading frames (< 100 amino acids).
claims.source: However, based on transcriptomes from D. simulans and D. mauritiana testes, we suspect that more than half of the duplicated genes are likely pseudogenes that either show no expression in testes ( < 3 TPM) or lack open reading frames ( < 100 amino acids; Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on transcriptome data.

claims.claim: Intrachromosomal duplications of Y-linked pseudogenes were detected, suggesting a high duplication rate within these Y chromosomes.
claims.source: We also detect intrachromosomal duplications of these Y-linked pseudogenes (Supplementary file 7), suggesting a high duplication rate within these Y chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data, with an inference about duplication rate.

claims.claim: Most new Y-linked duplications in D. melanogaster and the D. simulans clade are from genes with presumed functions in chromatin modification, cell division, and sexual reproduction.
claims.source: Most new Y-linked duplications in D. melanogaster and the D. simulans clade are from genes with presumed functions in chromatin modification, cell division, and sexual reproduction (Supplementary file 8), consistent with other Drosophila species (Bachtrog et al., 2019; Mahajan and Bachtrog, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on GO term analysis, consistent with previous research.

claims.claim: A duplication bias could contribute to the enrichment of Y-linked duplicates of genes with functions in chromatin modification, cell division, and sexual reproduction, as genes expressed in the testes may be more likely to duplicate to the Y chromosome due to its open chromatin structure and transcriptional activity during spermatogenesis.
claims.source: While Y-linked duplicates of genes with these functions may be selectively beneficial, a duplication bias could also contribute to this enrichment, as genes expressed in the testes may be more likely to duplicate to the Y chromosome due to its open chromatin structure and transcriptional activity during spermatogenesis (Greil and Ahmad, 2012; Mahadevaraju et al., 2021; Hess and Meyer, 1968).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Two new gene families have undergone extensive amplification on D. simulans clade Y chromosomes.
claims.source: We discovered two new gene families that have undergone extensive amplification on D. simulans clade Y chromosomes (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: Both new Y-linked gene families appear to encode functional protein-coding genes with complete open reading frames and high expression in mRNA-seq data.
claims.source: Both families appear to encode functional protein-coding genes with complete open reading frames and high expression in mRNA-seq data (Supplementary file 9) and have 36–146 copies in each species' Y chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The new Y-linked gene families have 36–146 copies in each species' Y chromosome.
claims.source: Both families appear to encode functional protein-coding genes with complete open reading frames and high expression in mRNA-seq data (Supplementary file 9) and have 36–146 copies in each species' Y chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: >90% of the variants in the assembled Y-linked gene families are represented in Illumina DNA-seq data.
claims.source: We also confirm that >90% of the variants in our assembled Y-linked gene families are represented in Illumina DNA-seq data (Appendix 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on validation with Illumina data.

claims.claim: The first amplified Y-linked gene family, SR Protein Kinase (SRPK), is derived from an autosome-to-Y duplication of the sequence encoding the testis-specific isoform of the gene SR Protein Kinase (SRPK).
claims.source: The first amplified Y-linked gene family, SR Protein Kinase (SRPK), is derived from an autosome-to-Y duplication of the sequence encoding the testis-specific isoform of the gene SR Protein Kinase (SRPK).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: After the duplication of SRPK to the Y chromosome, the ancestral autosomal copy subsequently lost its testis-specific exon via a deletion.
claims.source: After the duplication of SRPK to the Y chromosome, the ancestral autosomal copy subsequently lost its testis-specific exon via a deletion (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on phylogenetic and sequence analysis.

claims.claim: In D. melanogaster, SRPK is essential for both male and female reproduction.
claims.source: In D. melanogaster, SRPK is essential for both male and female reproduction (Loh et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The relocation of the testis-specific isoform of SRPK to the D. simulans clade Y chromosomes may have resolved intralocus sexual antagonism over male and female reproductive functions.
claims.source: We therefore hypothesize that the relocation of the testis-specific isoform to the D. simulans clade Y chromosomes may have resolved intralocus sexual antagonism over these two functions.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings of the study.

claims.claim: Phylogenetic analysis identified two subfamilies of Lhk designated Lhk-1 and Lhk-2.
claims.source: Our phylogenetic analysis identified two subfamilies of Lhk that we designate Lhk-1 and Lhk-2 (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Both Lhk subfamilies are shared by all D. simulans clade species and show a 5.5% protein divergence between species.
claims.source: Both subfamilies are shared by all D. simulans clade species and show a 5.5% protein divergence between species.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The two Lhk subfamilies are found in different locations in the Y chromosome assemblies.
claims.source: The two subfamilies are found in different locations in our Y chromosome assemblies; consistent with this observation, we detect two to three Lhk foci on Y chromosomes in the D. simulans clade using FISH (Figure 6A and C and Figure 1—figure supplements 3–4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly and FISH data.

claims.claim: Two to three Lhk foci are detected on Y chromosomes in the D. simulans clade using FISH.
claims.source: The two subfamilies are found in different locations in our Y chromosome assemblies; consistent with this observation, we detect two to three Lhk foci on Y chromosomes in the D. simulans clade using FISH (Figure 6A and C and Figure 1—figure supplements 3–4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on FISH data.

claims.claim: The second amplified gene family comprises both X-linked and Y-linked duplicates of the Ssl gene located on chromosome 2R.
claims.source: The second amplified gene family comprises both X-linked and Y-linked duplicates of the Ssl gene located on chromosome 2 R; it is unclear whether the X- or Y-linked copies originated first (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: It is unclear whether the X- or Y-linked copies of the Ssl gene family originated first.
claims.source: The second amplified gene family comprises both X-linked and Y-linked duplicates of the Ssl gene located on chromosome 2 R; it is unclear whether the X- or Y-linked copies originated first (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the uncertainty in the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The X-linked copies of the Ssl gene family are known as CK2ßtes-like in D. simulans.
claims.source: The X-linked copies are known as CK2ßtes-like in D. simulans (Kogan et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The Y-linked copies of the Ssl gene family are also found in D. melanogaster but are degenerated and have little or no expression.
claims.source: The Y-linked copies are also found in D. melanogaster but are degenerated and have little or no expression (Chang and Larracuente, 2019; Danilevskaya et al., 1991), leading to their designation as pseudogenes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: In the D. simulans clade species, the Y-linked paralogs of Ssl have high levels of expression (> 50 TPM in testes) and complete open reading frames.
claims.source: In the D. simulans clade species, however, the Y-linked paralogs have high levels of expression ( > 50 TPM in testes, Supplementary file 9) and complete open reading frames, so we refer to this gene family as CK2ßtes-Y.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Both CK2ßtes-like (4–9 copies) and CK2ßtes-Y (36–123 copies based on the assemblies) are amplified on the X and Y chromosome in the D. simulans clade relative to D. melanogaster.
claims.source: Both CK2ßtes-like (4–9 copies) and CK2ßtes-Y (36–123 copies based on the assemblies) are amplified on the X and Y chromosome in the D. simulans clade relative to D. melanogaster (Supplementary file 9; Kogan et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly data.

claims.claim: The Y-linked copies in D. melanogaster, Su(Ste), are known to be a source of piRNAs.
claims.source: The Y-linked copies in D. melanogaster, Su(Ste), are known to be a source of piRNAs (Aravin et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: No testis piRNAs from either CK2ßtes-like or CK2ßtes-Y gene family were detected in two small RNA-seq datasets.
claims.source: We did not detect any testis piRNAs from either gene family in two small RNA-seq datasets (SRR7410589 and SRR7410590); however, we do find some short ( < 23 nt) reads (0.003–0.005% of total mapped reads) mapped to these gene families (Supplementary file 10).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on small RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Some short (< 23 nt) reads (0.003–0.005% of total mapped reads) mapped to the CK2ßtes-like and CK2ßtes-Y gene families.
claims.source: We did not detect any testis piRNAs from either gene family in two small RNA-seq datasets (SRR7410589 and SRR7410590); however, we do find some short ( < 23 nt) reads (0.003–0.005% of total mapped reads) mapped to these gene families (Supplementary file 10).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on small RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: D. simulans clade species show similar gene conversion rates (on the order of 10–4 to 10–6) in both Lhk and CK2ßtes-Y families compared to previous estimates in D. melanogaster.
claims.source: In general, D. simulans clade species show similar gene conversion rates (on the order of 10–4 to 10–6) in both of these families compared to our previous estimates in D. melanogaster (Chang and Larracuente, 2019; Supplementary file 11).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Higher gene conversion rates on Y chromosomes compared to other chromosomes might be a shared feature of Y chromosomes across taxa.
claims.source: These higher gene conversion rates compared to the other chromosomes might be a shared feature of Y chromosomes across taxa (Rozen et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: After the divergence of D. simulans clade species, Lhk-1 evolved under purifying selection, whereas Lhk-2 evolved under positive selection.
claims.source: We infer that after the divergence of D. simulans clade species, Lhk-1 evolved under purifying selection, whereas Lhk-2 evolved under positive selection (Figure 6A; Table 2; Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 12).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on PAML analysis.

claims.claim: Highly expressed Lhk-1 copies have fewer nonsynonymous mutations than lowly expressed copies in D. simulans, consistent with purifying selection.
claims.source: Using transcriptome data, we observe that highly expressed Lhk-1 copies have fewer nonsynonymous mutations than lowly expressed copies in D. simulans, consistent with purifying selection (Chi-square test's p = 0.01; Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 13).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on transcriptome and DNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Both Lhk gene families are expressed two- to seven-fold higher than the ancestral copy on 2R in the same species.
claims.source: Both Lhk gene families are expressed two- to seven-fold higher than the ancestral copy on 2R in the same species, and 1.9–64-fold higher than their ortholog, SRPK-RC, in D. melanogaster, suggesting that gene amplification may confer increased expression.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Both Lhk gene families are expressed 1.9–64-fold higher than their ortholog, SRPK-RC, in D. melanogaster.
claims.source: Both Lhk gene families are expressed two- to seven-fold higher than the ancestral copy on 2R in the same species, and 1.9–64-fold higher than their ortholog, SRPK-RC, in D. melanogaster, suggesting that gene amplification may confer increased expression.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Gene amplification may confer increased expression of Lhk gene families.
claims.source: Both Lhk gene families are expressed two- to seven-fold higher than the ancestral copy on 2R in the same species, and 1.9–64-fold higher than their ortholog, SRPK-RC, in D. melanogaster, suggesting that gene amplification may confer increased expression.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed expression levels.

claims.claim: In both D. simulans and D. mauritiana, Lhk-1 is shorter due to deletions following its origin and has a higher expression level than Lhk-2.
claims.source: In both D. simulans and D. mauritiana, Lhk-1 is shorter due to deletions following its origin and has a higher expression level than Lhk-2.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Both Lhk gene families have higher copy numbers in D. simulans than D. mauritiana, which likely contributes to their higher expression level in D. simulans.
claims.source: Both Lhk gene families have higher copy numbers in D. simulans than D. mauritiana, which likely contributes to their higher expression level in D. simulans (Supplementary file 9).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on assembly and RNA-seq data, with an inference about the relationship between copy number and expression.

claims.claim: For both Lhk-1 and Lhk-2, copies from the same species are more similar than copies from other species—a signal of concerted evolution.
claims.source: For both Lhk-1 and Lhk-2, copies from the same species are more similar than copies from other species—a signal of concerted evolution (Dover, 1982).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on phylogenetic analysis, with a citation to the concept of concerted evolution.

claims.claim: The ancestral Ssl gene experienced a slightly increased rate of protein evolution after it duplicated to the X and Y chromosomes (ω = 0.41 vs 0.23; p = 0.03).
claims.source: The ancestral Ssl gene experienced a slightly increased rate of protein evolution after it duplicated to the X and Y chromosomes (ω = 0.41 vs 0.23; p = 0.03; Figure 6B; Table 2; Figure 6—figure supplement 3; Supplementary file 14).

results.result: The study generated improved Y chromosome assemblies for three D. simulans clade species using heterochromatin-enriched long-read sequencing methods, recovering 13.7-18.9 Mb of Y-linked sequences with N50 values of 0.6-1.2 Mb and achieving 96-99% sensitivity in chromosome assignments.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C45 collectively demonstrate successful assembly of Y chromosomes with quantified metrics (Table 1, assembly statistics) and validation through FISH cytology. The methods show clear improvement over previous assemblies (C35, C36), with specific sensitivity/specificity values provided (C39) and concordance between assembly and cytological data (C45). The technical validation is comprehensive.

results.result: Y chromosomes of the D. simulans clade species show extensive structural rearrangements including changes in satellite distribution, gene order, and centromere position, despite diverging only 250,000 years ago.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are directly supported by Figure 1 and FISH data showing dramatic rearrangements. C48 provides comparison with previous work, though C49 acknowledges uncertainty about D. sechellia centromere position. The rapid divergence despite recent speciation (C47) is well-documented through both assembly and cytological evidence.

results.result: Y-linked rDNA (28S) was lost in D. simulans and D. sechellia but retained in D. mauritiana, while IGS repeats are retained in all three species, though below FISH detection in D. sechellia.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by assembly data (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) and consistent with previous cytological studies (C50, C52 cite prior work). The inference about IGS abundance in D. sechellia (C54) is reasonable given assembly detection but FISH non-detection, representing appropriate interpretation of complementary data.

results.result: All three D. simulans clade species have at least one intact copy of 11 canonical Y-linked genes, but show extensive copy number variation in Y-linked exons, with some duplicates appearing functional based on expression and complete ORFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C66 are supported by assembly data (Figure 2) and RNA-seq validation (C60, C65, C66). The study provides both genomic evidence (assembly) and transcriptomic evidence (expression levels) for copy number variation. The inference about functionality (C59) is appropriately cautious, based on expression and ORF completeness. Illumina validation (C58) strengthens assembly-based claims.

results.result: Exon-intron junctions are conserved within full-length copies of canonical Y-linked genes, but intron lengths vary between species, with longer introns showing more dynamic length variation that cannot be attributed to single deletion/duplication events.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by assembly data (Figure 3) and sequence alignments (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). The observation about intron length dynamics (C70) is quantified, and the inference about multiple events (C71) is supported by alignment evidence showing complex patterns rather than simple indels.

results.result: Only the kl-3 mega-intron with (AATAT)n repeats is conserved across all four species, while (AAGAC)n repeats are missing from D. simulans clade genomes, suggesting that mega-introns and Y-loops turn over at both sequence and gene levels over short evolutionary time.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 are supported by assembly data, Illumina reads (Supplementary file 6), and published FISH results (C80). The inference about turnover (C83) is reasonable given the ~2 My divergence time and observed sequence-level changes. The conclusion is appropriately cautious ('may be conserved features' but 'turn over').

results.result: The study identified 49 independent duplications to the Y chromosome in the D. simulans clade (including 8 newly discovered), with a transposition rate 3-4 times higher than D. melanogaster, and inferred 17 independent deletions.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 4) and assembly data. The classification of duplication mechanisms (C87) and rate comparison (C88) are quantified. The inference of deletions (C89) is based on phylogenetic reconstruction, which is an appropriate method for this analysis.

results.result: Two new Y-linked gene families (Lhk and CK2βtes-Y) were discovered with 36-146 copies per species, showing complete ORFs and high expression, with Lhk derived from autosome-to-Y duplication of testis-specific SRPK isoform followed by loss of the testis-specific exon in the autosomal copy.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 are supported by assembly data (Figure 5), RNA-seq data showing high expression (C96), and Illumina validation (C98: >90% variants confirmed). The phylogenetic reconstruction of Lhk origin (C99-C100) is supported by sequence analysis and gene structure comparison. This represents a major discovery of novel gene families.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis identified two Lhk subfamilies (Lhk-1 and Lhk-2) with 5.5% protein divergence between species, located at different Y chromosome positions, with Lhk-1 evolving under purifying selection and Lhk-2 under positive selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 6A) and FISH data confirming 2-3 foci. The selection inference (C118) is supported by PAML analysis (Table 2), and C119 provides additional transcriptome-based evidence for purifying selection on Lhk-1 (Chi-square test p=0.01). The statistical support is appropriate.

results.result: The second amplified gene family comprises X-linked (CK2βtes-like) and Y-linked (CK2βtes-Y) duplicates of Ssl, with Y-linked copies showing high expression (>50 TPM) in D. simulans clade but degenerated in D. melanogaster, and both showing strong positive selection (p=8.8E-9).
results.evaluation: Claims C107, C111-C112 are supported by assembly and RNA-seq data. The positive selection inference (C126-C127) is supported by PAML analysis with highly significant p-values (Table 2, Figure 6B). The contrast with D. melanogaster (degenerated Y-linked copies) provides evolutionary context. Statistical evidence is strong.

results.result: D. simulans clade species show gene conversion rates of 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁶ in Lhk and CK2βtes-Y families, similar to D. melanogaster, with copies from the same species being more similar than copies from other species, indicating concerted evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C116 and C125 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Supplementary file 11) using established methods (four-gamete tests, gene similarity). The concerted evolution inference (C125) is appropriately supported by within-species similarity patterns. The comparison to D. melanogaster provides context for interpreting the rates.

results.result: Y chromosomes show proportionally more large deletions (25.1% of indels ≥10 bp) compared to other chromosomes in both D. melanogaster and D. simulans, with this pattern shared across D. simulans clade Y chromosomes but not driven by heterochromatin or lack of recombination, suggesting preferential use of MMEJ over NHEJ.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C137 are supported by quantified indel analysis (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 15) with statistical significance (p<1e-6). The control comparisons (C138-C140) using dot chromosome and heterochromatic pseudogenes appropriately rule out alternative explanations. The MMEJ inference (C142-C143) is supported by microhomology analysis showing 39.5-57% of deletions have ≥2 bp microhomology, consistent with MMEJ mechanism.

results.result: Five new Y-linked satellites were discovered spanning 5,515-26,119 bp, with one (AAACAT)n originating from a DM412B transposable element and expanding to 764 copies specifically in D. mauritiana.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C147 are supported by assembly data and FISH validation (Figure 1—figure supplements 3-4, Supplementary file 6). The origin of (AAACAT)n from TE (C146) is supported by flanking sequence analysis. The species-specific expansion in D. mauritiana (C147) is quantified. This represents a solid discovery of novel satellite sequences.

results.result: D. simulans clade Y chromosomes are enriched for LTR retrotransposons that turn over between species, with positive correlation (rho=0.45-0.50) between Y-linked TE abundance differences and genome-wide differences when comparing to D. melanogaster, but weaker correlations within the clade (rho<0.23), suggesting some TEs shift insertion preferences.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C158 are supported by repeat annotation data (Supplementary files 17-18, Figure 7—figure supplements 1-3). The correlation analysis (C154, C156) provides quantitative support for the inference about global TE activity changes (C155) versus insertion preference shifts (C156-C157). The DIVER element example (C158) provides specific support. The analysis appropriately distinguishes between-clade and within-clade patterns.

results.result: The repair of double-strand breaks on Y chromosomes may be biased toward MMEJ over NHEJ based on four lines of evidence: lack of X homology precluding homologous recombination, exclusion of Ku complex from HP1a-rich regions, high repetitive content increasing DSB formation, and observed high duplication/gene conversion rates with large deletion sizes.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C166 present a mechanistic model supported by multiple lines of evidence. C162 states established fact about Y chromosome biology. C163-C165 cite previous research about DNA repair mechanisms. C166 integrates the study's empirical findings (high duplication rates, gene conversion, large deletions from C136-C143) with the mechanistic model. While the model is inferential (C8, C134), it is well-supported by converging evidence and appropriately presented as a proposal (C161).

results.result: The relocation of testis-specific SRPK isoform to Y chromosomes may have resolved intralocus sexual antagonism, and co-amplification of sex-linked genes (CK2βtes-like/CK2βtes-Y) with positive selection may result from arms race between sex chromosome drivers, with systems potentially shifting from protein-coding to RNA-based mechanisms over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C102, C129-C130, C185, C187, C190-C191 are explicitly speculative (using 'may,' 'might,' 'suspect,' 'propose,' 'speculate'). While the speculation is informed by the data (positive selection on CK2βtes genes, homology to Stellate/Su(Ste) system), these are hypotheses rather than demonstrated results. The functional claims lack direct experimental validation of sexual antagonism or meiotic drive. The evolutionary scenario is plausible but not directly tested.

results.result: New Y-linked gene families (Lhk and CK2βtes-Y) evolved under both positive selection and gene conversion, suggesting that high copy numbers and Y-Y gene conversion are important for adaptation of new Y-linked genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C118, C127 are supported by PAML analysis showing positive selection (Table 2) with significant p-values. C181 represents an inference from the combined evidence of positive selection, gene conversion, and high copy numbers. While the inference about 'importance' is somewhat speculative, it is well-grounded in the empirical findings and represents a reasonable synthesis of the data.

results.result: The analyses provide a link between Y-linked mutation patterns and Y chromosome evolution, with high gene duplication and gene conversion rates potentially countering reduced selection efficacy, and unique mutation patterns possibly resulting from heterochromatic environment, predicting similar patterns in W chromosomes and non-recombining sex-limited chromosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C192-C195 represent high-level synthesis and predictions. C192-C193 are reasonable inferences from the study's findings, but C194-C195 are explicitly speculative predictions about mechanisms and other systems. While the prediction about W chromosomes is partially supported by cited evidence (C196), the causal claim about heterochromatin (C194) lacks direct experimental validation. These represent important hypotheses but are not fully demonstrated.
